metaTitle: Mortgage Redemption Suit Law in Bangladesh
title: Mortgage Redemption Suit Law in Bangladesh
metaDescription: Reclaim mortgaged land or prevent unlawful foreclosure in Bangladesh under Sections 60 & 83 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882. Learn 60-year rules.
keywords: Section 83 Transfer of Property Act deposit
heroIntro: Under Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, any borrower or landowner who mortgaged immovable property retains an absolute statutory 'Right of Redemption'—even after the due date passes—until extinguished by court decree or valid registered act. Under Article 148 of the Limitation Act, 1908, a mortgagor has up to 60 years to sue for redemption and recover possession.

quickAnswer.heading: At a Glance: Mortgage Redemption in Bangladesh
points: Governing Laws: Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (Sections 58, 60, 62, 83 & 91) & Limitation Act, 1908 (Article 148).
Limitation Period: 60 years from when the right to redeem or recover possession accrues (Article 148).
Court Deposit Option: Deposit remaining principal + interest in court under Section 83 TP Act if the lender refuses repayment.
Clog on Redemption Void: Any contract clause permanently blocking redemption upon late payment ('once a mortgage, always a mortgage') is void.

sections.h2: Right of Redemption Under Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act
sections.content:
Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 guarantees that at any time after the principal money has become due, the mortgagor has a statutory right, on payment or tender of the mortgage money, to require the mortgagee to deliver back the mortgage deed and all title documents, restore possession of the property, and execute a registered re-transfer or acknowledgement of discharge.

In rural and urban Bangladesh alike, lenders frequently draft harsh conditions claiming that if the loan is not repaid by a fixed date, the mortgage automatically converts into an outright sale. Bangladeshi courts strictly enforce the equitable maxim 'once a mortgage, always a mortgage'—striking down any clog on the equity of redemption as void under Section 60.

Whether your dispute involves a private usufructuary mortgage or a bank security, consult a property lawyer in Bangladesh or review bank auction stay remedies in Artha Rin Adalat.

sections.h2: Types of Mortgages and Usufructuary (Khai-Khalashi) Rules
sections.content:
Section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 recognises six categories of mortgages in Bangladesh, each carrying distinct possession and redemption rules under Section 62 and the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.

Mortgage Type (Sec. 58)Possession & RegistrationRedemption Rule in Bangladesh
Simple MortgagePossession stays with borrower; must be registered under Sec. 59.Redeemable within 60 years by paying principal + agreed interest.
Mortgage by Conditional SaleOstensive sale deed with condition to reconvey on repayment (must be in same deed).Remains a redeemable mortgage unless foreclosed by court decree.
Usufructuary MortgageLender takes possession and enjoys rent/crops in lieu of interest.Under Section 95A SAT Act (Khai-Khalashi), agricultural usufructuary mortgages extinguish automatically after 7 years.
Equitable Mortgage (Title Deeds)Deposit of original title deeds in notified towns (e.g., Dhaka, Chattogram).Common in bank loans; redeemed upon bank NOC and return of original deeds.

Note that under Section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, if an owner entered a kot-kabala or conditional sale of agricultural land with possession, it is treated as a complete usufructuary mortgage expiring automatically after 7 years—even if disguised as an out-and-out sale with a separate reconveyance agreement. Check khatian records online if a lender mutated your land improperly.

sections.h2: 60-Year Limitation and Clog on Redemption Doctrine
sections.content:
Under Article 148 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908, a suit against a mortgagee to redeem or to recover possession of immovable property mortgaged enjoys a generous 60-year limitation period from when the right to redeem or recover possession accrues.

Even if the borrower misses the contractual due date by several years, the right of redemption under Section 60 survives intact until the mortgagee obtains a final decree of foreclosure or sells the property lawfully under a statutory power (such as an Artha Rin Adalat auction). Furthermore, under Section 91 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, not only the original borrower, but also any co-sharer, heir, subsequent purchaser, or surety may sue to redeem the mortgage.

If the lender forged a Saf Kabala sale deed instead of a registered mortgage, you may combine a deed cancellation suit under Section 39 Specific Relief Act with a redemption prayer.

sections.h2: Step-by-Step Procedure to Redeem Mortgaged Land in Court
sections.content:
If a private lender or bank refuses to accept full repayment and return your title deeds or land, follow this statutory sequence under Sections 60 and 83 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882:

  1. Serve Formal Tender Notice: Issue an advocate's notice offering exact principal and lawful interest, requesting return of original deeds and registered redemption/reconveyance within 15 days.
  2. Deposit Mortgage Money in Court (Section 83 TP Act): File a Miscellaneous Petition under Section 83 before the Assistant Judge or Joint District Judge Court depositing the remaining amount due; once the court serves notice on the mortgagee, interest stops running from the date of deposit (Section 84).
  3. File Redemption Suit (Order 34 Rules 7–8 CPC): If the mortgagee refuses to accept the Section 83 deposit or disputes accounts, file a regular civil suit for redemption and accounting under Order 34 CPC.
  4. Obtain Preliminary & Final Redemption Decrees: The court settles the exact balance due (crediting any rent/crops collected by a usufructuary mortgagee under Section 76) and passes a final decree ordering delivery of deeds and possession.
  5. Execute Possession & Update Mutation: Enforce the decree via court Nazir if the lender still resists, and restore Khajna/Namjari; Advocate Md. Shah Alam represents resident and NRB landowners in complex mortgage and kot-kabala recoveries.

sections.h2: Documents Checklist for a Mortgage Redemption Suit
sections.content:
Prepare these original and certified records to establish the mortgage terms and payments made:

  • Registered Mortgage Deed, Conditional Sale Deed, or Memorandum of Deposit of Title Deeds.
  • Photocopies of original title deeds, CS/SA/RS/BS Khatians, and Khajna receipts.
  • Loan repayment receipts, bank transfer slips, bKash/cheque stubs, or crop-sharing accounts.
  • Copy of the formal tender notice and Section 83 court deposit Treasury Challan (if already tendered).
  • For heirs or NRBs abroad: Warish Certificate and an Embassy-attested Power of Attorney.

faqs.question: Can a lender refuse to return my mortgaged land because I missed the repayment due date?
faqs.answer: No. Under Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the right of redemption continues even after the contractual repayment date passes, up to 60 years under Article 148 of the Limitation Act, 1908, unless extinguished by a court foreclosure decree or lawful auction.

faqs.question: What if a private lender refuses to accept my loan repayment in cash?
faqs.answer: You can file a petition under Section 83 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and deposit the entire balance due into the civil court. Under Section 84, interest ceases to run from the date of valid court deposit and notice to the lender.

faqs.question: Is a separate reconveyance agreement valid to prove a conditional sale was actually a mortgage?
faqs.answer: Under the proviso to Section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a transaction is only treated as a mortgage by conditional sale if the condition of reconveyance is embodied in the same document. However, for agricultural land, Section 95A of the SAT Act, 1950 still treats kot-kabala transfers with possession as 7-year usufructuary mortgages.

faqs.question: How long does a usufructuary (Khai-Khalashi) mortgage of agricultural land last in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Under Section 95 and Section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, a complete usufructuary mortgage of agricultural land automatically extinguishes after a maximum of 7 years, and the landowner is entitled to recover possession without paying any further principal.

faqs.question: Can legal heirs redeem a mortgage after the original borrower passes away?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Section 91 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, any legal heir, co-sharer, or person having an interest in the mortgaged property may file a Section 83 deposit or a civil redemption suit within the 60-year limitation period.
